newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA EDUCATION MINISTER UNHAPPY AT BUDGET SPLIT.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA EDUCATION MINISTER UNHAPPY AT BUDGET SPLIT.

text.p: Education Minister Sibusiso Bengu on Monday criticised South Africa's budgetary arrangements, saying they gave the individual provinces too much control over school spending.
"Our current budget process does not make space for the ministry to exert any direct influence on the total amounts to be voted for provincial education," Bengu said in a speech to parliament.
"That is not how it should be. We have not fought a fragmented... racial and ethnic system in order to embrace a fragmented ... national-provincial system," he said.

Before the all-race elections in April 1994, South Africa had separate education departments for each of the four provinces then in existence, separate departments for black and white scholars, and separate departments in the nine black homelands created under apartheid.
It now has a national ministry and separate departments for nine new provinces created in 1994.
In the constitutional negotiations leading up to the 1994 election, opposition parties pressed for an advanced degree of autonomy in education and other matters to be devolved to the provinces.
Two provinces are held by opposition parties -- Western Cape, where the National Party has a majority, and KwaZulu- Natal, where the Inkatha Freedom Party has a majority.
Bengu said education policy was too important to be jeopardised "by dogmatic insistence on unilateral provincial prerogatives".
"We have one, integrated, inter-dependent system. Let us, national and provincial governments, do the rational and far-sighted thing, and plan for its development and success together," he said.
Blade Nzimandi, African National Congress chairman of parliament's education committee, accused the National Party of pushing for provincial autonomy as a way of undermining "transformation".

"Now that they no longer control the state, they are seeking to turn these vestiges of apartheid privilege into centres of power that lie beyond the influence of the national government," he told the national assembly.
